text: Roadmapping -- turning business goals into a technical plan. Every lesson so far has worked from a technical starting point toward a decision. Roadmapping runs the opposite direction: starting from a business goal that says nothing technical at all, and turning it into a sequenced technical plan. That's the specific skill separating an engineer who executes well-defined tickets from one trusted to figure out what the tickets should even be.

Here's the goal, as leadership hands it down. Reduce customer support costs by twenty percent this year, primarily by deflecting more tickets to the AI assistant before they reach a human agent. That's a real, meaningful business goal -- and it contains zero technical specifics. Turning it into an actual roadmap is the Staff or Principal engineer's job, not leadership's.

Breaking it down produces candidate initiatives: improve retrieval quality, expand the knowledge base, add a confidence threshold that routes weak answers to a human, reduce response latency -- and, notably, refactor the duplicated prompt-assembly logic from an earlier lesson. That refactor is on the roadmap even though leadership never asked for it and it doesn't move the deflection-rate metric directly, because it's a real, identified dependency for the retrieval-quality work.

Listing initiatives is the easy part. Sequencing is where the real planning happens. The refactor has to happen before hybrid search, because hybrid search touches the exact code path the refactor cleans up -- build on top of the current duplicated logic and you're implementing it five times instead of once. The confidence-threshold work, by contrast, can run in parallel with either, since it shares no dependency with them.

Notice how much of this course already feeds into this one roadmap. Capacity planning tells you whether expanding the knowledge base pushes infrastructure past a ceiling partway through the year. Build-versus-buy applies directly to the retrieval work -- build a custom layer, or adopt a vendor's existing features. And the tech-debt break-even math is exactly what justifies the refactor's place on the roadmap even with no direct metric impact. Roadmapping isn't a separate skill learned from scratch -- it's where everything else in this course gets applied together, under one real business goal, at once.
Next up, the capstone: writing a real architecture decision record, applying this course's full toolkit to one unresolved decision, start to finish.
